rules.title: The ext2fs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The ext2fs filesystem module is used to read from or write to traditional Linux filesystems such as ext2/ext3/ext4.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. The module is only needed for temporary reading and writing of ext2/ext3/ext4 filesystems.

rules.title: The msdosfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The msdosfs driver allows the FreeBSD kernel to read and write filesystems based on MS-DOS.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. The module is only needed for MS-DOS-based filesystems such as FAT16 or FAT32, which appear on flash cards and other memory cards.

rules.title: The zfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The zfs filesystem is a scalable filesystem used in FreeBSD for large systems with huge disk spaces.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. The module is only required when ZFS storage systems are used or FreeBSD is installed on ZFS partitions.

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is world-writable and holds temporary files for all users and some applications. It can be mounted as tmpfs, whose size and inodes mount options limit the filesystem and can be changed on remount.
rules.impact: A separate /tmp filesystem allows mount options such as noexec, so an attacker cannot install or run code there, and blocks hard-link attacks on setuid programs that are later updated. This is achieved by mounting tmpfs at /tmp or by using a dedicated partition.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. It is useless if a publicly available suid or sgid wrapper is installed, and it is set automatically when the user lacks superuser privileges.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is intended only for temporary file storage, nosuid prevents users from creating setuid files there.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. It was not designed as a security feature, and scripts on a noexec-mounted partition can still be executed.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is intended only for temporary file storage, noexec prevents users from running executable binaries there.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory is used to support the needs of local users.
rules.impact: A separate /home filesystem allows additional mount options such as noexec, nosuid and nodev, and usrquota or grpquota to limit disk use. Without it, user data can fill the single default / partition and exhaust resources for the whole system.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /home partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. It is useless if a publicly available suid or sgid wrapper is installed, and it is set automatically when the user lacks superuser privileges.
rules.impact: Because /home is intended only for storing user files, nosuid prevents users from creating setuid files there.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and other system services for temporary storage of dynamic data. Some directories created by these processes may be world-writable.
rules.impact: A separate /var filesystem allows additional mount options such as noexec, nosuid and nodev, and prevents world-writable data from filling the root filesystem. It also blocks hard-link attacks on setuid programs that are later updated.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. It is useless if a publicly available suid or sgid wrapper is installed, and it is set automatically when the user lacks superuser privileges.
rules.impact: Because /var is intended only for variable files such as logs, nosuid prevents users from creating setuid files there.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is world-writable and holds temporary files for all users and some applications. Files there are preserved between reboots.
rules.impact: A separate /var/tmp filesystem allows additional mount options such as noexec and nosuid, and prevents world-writable temporary files from filling the root filesystem and disrupting daemons. It also blocks hard-link attacks on setuid programs that are later updated.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. It is useless if a publicly available suid or sgid wrapper is installed, and it is set automatically when the user lacks superuser privileges.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is intended only for temporary file storage, nosuid prevents users from creating setuid files there.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. It was not designed as a security feature, and scripts on a noexec-mounted partition can still be executed.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is intended only for temporary file storage, noexec prevents users from running executable binaries there.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: A separate /var/log filesystem allows additional mount options such as noexec and nosuid, and keeps log files that grow quite large from filling the root filesystem.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. It is useless if a publicly available suid or sgid wrapper is installed, and it is set automatically when the user lacks superuser privileges.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is intended only for log files, nosuid prevents users from creating setuid files there.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. It was not designed as a security feature, and scripts on a noexec-mounted partition can still be executed.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is intended only for log files, noexec prevents users from running executable binaries there.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/audit
rules.explanation: The audit daemon, auditd, stores log data in the /var/audit directory.
rules.impact: A separate /var/audit filesystem allows additional mount options such as noexec and nosuid, and keeps the growing audit log from filling the root filesystem.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/audit partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. It is useless if a publicly available suid or sgid wrapper is installed, and it is set automatically when the user lacks superuser privileges.
rules.impact: Because /var/audit is intended only for variable files such as logs, nosuid prevents users from creating setuid files there.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/audit partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. It was not designed as a security feature, and scripts on a noexec-mounted partition can still be executed.
rules.impact: Because /var/audit is intended only for audit logs, noexec prevents users from running executable binaries there.

rules.title: Update server certificate key fingerprints are configured
rules.explanation: FreeBSD downloads binary updates from an update server and verifies them using a public key infrastructure. The key fingerprint is set in /etc/freebsd-update.conf, varies between FreeBSD versions and must be verified manually.
rules.impact: A correctly configured key fingerprint protects against spoofing that could install malicious software through updates. The fingerprint in /etc/freebsd-update.conf is correct only if it matches the expected value for the installed version.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Systems should have the appropriate package manager repositories configured so that the latest fixes and updates are available.
rules.impact: Incorrectly configured system package repositories can hide important patches, and a rogue repository can introduce compromised software.

rules.title: Updates, patches, and additional security software are installed
rules.explanation: Fixes are released periodically for the included software, either because of security deficiencies or because of additional functionality.
rules.impact: New patches may contain security improvements that are not available through the last full update. Organizations need to determine whether a given update meets their requirements and to verify the compatibility of additional software.

rules.title: The bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: A bootloader password requires anyone rebooting the system to enter a password before setting boot command line parameters.
rules.impact: A boot password prevents an unauthorized user from changing boot parameters or the boot partition, including weakening security by reducing the kernel security level during boot.

rules.title: Permissions on the bootloader config are configured
rules.explanation: The loader.conf file contains information about boot settings and passwords for unlocking boot options.
rules.impact: Root-only read and write permissions prevent users from seeing or changing boot parameters. Non-root users who read the boot parameters may identify weaknesses in boot security and exploit them.

rules.title: Address space layout randomization (ASLR) is enabled
rules.explanation: Address space layout randomization (ASLR) is an exploit mitigation technique that randomly arranges the address space of key data areas of a process. It is enabled by default as of FreeBSD 13.2.
rules.impact: Random placement of virtual memory regions makes memory page exploits more difficult to write, because the memory placement constantly changes.

rules.title: Core dump backtraces are disabled
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program, usually used to determine why a program aborts. It can also be used to collect confidential information from the core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image taken when the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is generally useful only to developers trying to debug problems.

rules.title: Core dump storage is disabled
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program, usually used to determine why a program aborts. It can also be used to collect confidential information from the core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image taken when the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is usually useful only to developers trying to debug problems.

rules.title: The message of the day is configured properly
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file is displayed to users after login as the message of the day. Unix-based systems typically display operating system release and patch level information at login.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users of their legal status with respect to the system and should name the organization that owns it and any monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch level information gives attackers detail that helps them target specific exploits.

rules.title: The local login warning banner is configured properly
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file is displayed before login on local terminals. FreeBSD does not use the file by default, and sshd must be configured properly to use /etc/issue.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users of their legal status with respect to the system and should name the organization that owns it and any monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch level information gives attackers detail that helps them target specific exploits.

rules.title: The remote login warning banner is configured properly
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue.net file is displayed before login for remote connections from configured services. FreeBSD does not use it by default; it is only needed for telnetd or ftpd.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users of their legal status with respect to the system and should name the organization that owns it and any monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch level information gives attackers detail that helps them target specific exploits.

rules.title: Access to /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file is displayed to users after login as the message of the day.
rules.impact: If /etc/motd has the wrong access, unauthorized users can modify it with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file is displayed before login on local terminals.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue has the wrong access, unauthorized users can modify it with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Time synchronization is in use
rules.explanation: System time is synchronized by a service such as the NTP daemon, ntpd, or chrony, which keeps clocks aligned to an accurate source; NTP can act as a client or a server.
rules.impact: Time synchronization supports time-sensitive security mechanisms such as Kerberos and keeps log entries consistent across the enterprise, which helps forensic investigations.

rules.title: The autofs services are not in use
rules.explanation: The autofs service allows automatic mounting of devices, which typically include CD/DVD and USB drives.
rules.impact: With automount enabled, anyone with physical access can attach a USB drive or disk and have its contents available, even without permission to mount it.

rules.title: The ftp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: FTP is a traditional protocol for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, including anonymous access without authentication. FreeBSD ships a basic ftpd in the base system and vsftpd as a package.
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or of authentication credentials. If the system is not needed as an FTP server, removing the package reduces the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The message access server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The dovecot and cyrus-imapd services are open source IMAP and POP3 server packages.
rules.impact: If POP3 or IMAP service is not provided by this system, removing the package reduces the potential attack surface. Other IMAP/POP3 servers may use different service names and should also be checked.

rules.title: The network file system services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Network File System (NFS) lets systems mount filesystems of other servers over the network. FreeBSD ships the NFS server in the base system, disabled.
rules.impact: If the system does not require network shares or the ability to serve filesystems to other hosts, disabling the nfsd service reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: The nis server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Network Information Service (NIS), formerly Yellow Pages, is a client-server directory service protocol for distributing system configuration files. The client, ypbind, binds a machine to an NIS server.
rules.impact: NIS is inherently insecure: it is vulnerable to denial of service attacks and buffer overflows and has poor authentication for querying NIS maps. LDAP usually replaces it, and FreeBSD ships the NIS server disabled by default.

rules.title: The rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rpcbind utility maps RPC services to the ports they listen on: RPC processes register their ports and program numbers, and clients are redirected to the correct port. Portmapper always listens on TCP and UDP port 111 and maps services such as nfs, nlockmgr, quotad and mountd.
rules.impact: A small request of about 82 bytes over UDP to Portmapper generates a response 7 to 28 times larger, which makes it suitable for DDoS amplification attacks. FreeBSD ships rpcbind in the base system, disabled by default.

rules.title: The snmp services are not in use
rules.explanation: SNMP is a widely used protocol for monitoring network equipment, computer equipment and devices such as UPSs. Net-SNMP implements SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 over IPv4 and IPv6.
rules.impact: The SNMP server can use SNMPv1, which transmits data in clear text and does not require authentication to execute commands. If SNMP is not required, removing the net-snmp package reduces the attack surface; otherwise the server should use SNMPv3 with authentication and message encryption.

rules.title: The telnet server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The freebsd-telnetd package contains the telnet daemon, which accepts connections from users on other systems via the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted, so a user able to sniff network traffic can steal credentials. The ssh service provides an encrypted session and stronger protection.

rules.title: The tftp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP machines, and TFTP servers let clients send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control or authentication, which allows an attacker to use it to gain access to files. FreeBSD ships tftpd in the base system, served through inetd and disabled by default.

rules.title: The web proxy server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Squid is the standard proxy server used in many distributions and environments.
rules.impact: If the system is not specifically configured as a proxy server, removing the squid package reduces the potential attack surface. Other HTTP proxy servers should be checked and removed if not required.

rules.title: Mail transfer agents are configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: Mail transfer agents (MTAs) such as sendmail and Postfix listen for incoming mail and transfer messages to the appropriate user or mail server. An MTA on a system that is not a mail server is configured to handle local mail only.
rules.impact: MTA software is complex and most of it has a long history of security problems. An MTA daemon listening on a port is unnecessary when the server does not receive and process mail from other systems.

rules.title: Only approved services are listening on a network interface
rules.explanation: A listening port is a network port on which an application or process listens, identified by its number, IP address and protocol such as TCP or UDP. An open port accepts incoming packets from remote locations.
rules.impact: Listening services on the system represent a potential attack vector. Services that are not required should be stopped and the package that contains the service removed.

rules.title: IPv6 status is identified
rules.explanation: Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) is the most recent version of the Internet Protocol, using 128-bit addressing to support the predicted growth of connected devices. It adds hierarchical addressing and routing, stateful and stateless configuration support and QoS support.
rules.impact: IETF RFC 4038 recommends that applications be built with dual stack. If dual stack and IPv6 are not used in the environment, IPv6 can be disabled to reduce the attack surface; otherwise it should be enabled and configured in line with site policy.

rules.title: The sctp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a transport layer protocol for message-oriented communication with multiple streams of messages in a single connection. It is message-oriented like UDP and provides reliable transport with congestion control like TCP.
rules.impact: If the protocol is not used, leaving the sctp kernel module unloaded reduces the potential attack surface.

rules.title: IP forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The net.inet.ip.forwarding and net.inet6.ip6.forwarding flags tell the system whether it can forward packets. The gateway and ipv6 gateway services do the same thing behind the scenes.
rules.impact: Setting both flags to 0 prevents a system with multiple interfaces, such as a hard proxy, from forwarding packets, so it never acts as a router. The gateway and ipv6 gateway services must also be disabled.

rules.title: Packet redirect sending is disabled
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects are used to send routing information to other hosts. A host that does not act as a router has no need to send redirects.
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send invalid ICMP redirects to router devices and corrupt routing, sending traffic to a system the attacker controls instead of the valid system.

rules.title: Broadcast and multicast ICMP requests are ignored
rules.explanation: An ICMP broadcast request goes to all hosts in a subnet for diagnostics such as host discovery, and a multicast request targets a specific group of subscriber hosts. This setting makes the system ignore all ICMP echo and timestamp requests to broadcast and multicast addresses.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP echo and timestamp requests with broadcast or multicast destinations can involve the host in a Smurf attack. Such an attack sends many ICMP messages with a spoofed source address, and the replies flood that address.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages convey routing information and tell the host, acting as a router, to send packets along an alternative path, which allows an external routing device to update the routing tables of the system.
rules.impact: Setting net.inet.icmp.drop_redirect to 1 and net.inet6.icmp6.rediraccept to 0 makes the system accept no ICMP redirect messages, so outside users cannot update its routing tables.

rules.title: Source routed packets are not accepted
rules.explanation: Source routing in a network allows the sender to partially or fully specify the route that packets take. Packets that are not source routed follow the path determined by the routers in the network.
rules.impact: Setting net.inet.ip.accept_sourceroute to 0 disables the system from accepting source routed packets. Without it, an attacker on the Internet could specify a route into private address systems that normal routing would not reach.

rules.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled
rules.explanation: When net.inet.tcp.syncookies is set, the kernel answers a SYN with a SYN/ACK carrying a crafted sequence number that encodes the source and destination IP address, the port and the time, without using the SYN queue. A valid ACK verifies the response and allows the connection even with no matching SYN in the queue.
rules.impact: SYN attacks send a large number of SYN packets without completing the handshake, which exhausts the half-open connection queue and prevents legitimate connections. Setting net.inet.tcp.syncookies to 1 keeps the system accepting valid connections during such an attack.

rules.title: IPv6 router advertisements are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMPv6 router advertisements tell hosts on the local network how to acquire a global unicast IPv6 address and provide information about the local router and default gateway. This setting disables the ability of the system to accept IPv6 router advertisements.
rules.impact: A rogue RA can make dual-stack nodes use the attacker system as their default gateway, enabling a man-in-the-middle attack, and can destabilize existing IPv6 networks. Setting net.inet6.ip6.accept_rtadv to 0 prevents router advertisements from being accepted, which is the FreeBSD default.

rules.title: IPFW is enabled and configured
rules.explanation: The ipfw interface is a packet classification framework in the kernel, based on the network virtual machine and the ipfw userspace command-line tool. It reuses existing dummynet subsystems such as the hook infrastructure, connection tracking, NAT and userspace queueing and logging.
rules.impact: ipfw is a FreeBSD kernel subsystem that protects against threats originating from the corporate network, including malicious mobile code and poorly configured software on the host.

rules.title: A single firewall utility is in use
rules.explanation: FreeBSD ships several firewall utilities, offering usage options that best suit their environment. This section provides guidance on implementing only one firewall utility.
rules.impact: Using more than one firewall utility can lead to unexpected results.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/crontab are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file is used by cron to control its own jobs, and root must be the user and group owner with access limited to the owner.
rules.impact: The file contains information about which system jobs cron runs. Access may give unprivileged users the ability to escalate their privileges, or insight into the operation of the system and a way to obtain unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.d are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory contains system cron jobs that run like the hourly, daily, weekly and monthly jobs from /etc/crontab but need more granular control over when they run. Its files cannot be managed with the crontab command and are edited by system administrators with a text editor.
rules.impact: Write access to this directory for unprivileged users may give them the means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Access may also give an unprivileged user insight into how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Crontab is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: The crontab program installs, deinstalls or lists the tables that drive the cron daemon, and the root administrator is always allowed to use it. If /var/cron/allow exists, a user must be listed in it, otherwise /var/cron/deny applies, allow takes precedence when both exist, and both files must be world-readable.
rules.impact: On many systems only the system administrator has the right to schedule jobs, and an allow file enforces this policy. An allow list is easier to manage than a deny list, where a user ID may be added to the system and forgotten in the deny file.

rules.title: The at utility is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: The at utility runs jobs at a specified time, and the superuser can always use it. Other users need a name in /var/at/at.allow if that file exists or must be absent from /var/at/at.deny, and if neither file exists only the superuser may use at, which is the default configuration.
rules.impact: On many systems only the system administrator has the right to schedule work, and an at.allow file enforces this policy. An allow list is easier to manage than a deny list, where a user ID may be added to the system and forgotten in the deny file.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/ssh/sshd_config are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file contains configuration specifications for sshd.
rules.impact: The configuration specifications of sshd must be protected from unauthorized changes by unprivileged users.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH private host key files are configured
rules.explanation: The SSH private key is one of two files used in SSH public key authentication, where possession of the private key is proof of identity and only the key matching the public key authenticates successfully. Copies of the private key must not be distributed.
rules.impact: If an unauthorized user obtains the private SSH host key file, the host can be impersonated.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH public host key files are configured
rules.explanation: The SSH public key is one of two files used in SSH public key authentication, and it verifies digital signatures generated with the corresponding private key. Only the public key that matches the private key authenticates successfully.
rules.impact: If the host public key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised.

rules.title: Sshd access is configured
rules.explanation: The AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers and DenyGroups options restrict access of users and groups to the system over SSH, and at least one of them is recommended. AllowUsers and DenyUsers take space-separated user names or user@host entries, and AllowGroups and DenyGroups take space-separated group names.
rules.impact: Restricting the access of users to the system over SSH helps ensure that only authorized users have access to the system.

rules.title: Sshd Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents are sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn users connecting to a particular site about the connection policy. A warning message before the normal login may help the prosecution of intruders.

rules.title: Sshd Ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: This variable limits the ciphers that SSH can use during communication, and some organizations have stricter requirements for approved ciphers. The only strong ciphers compatible with FIPS 140-2 are aes256-ctr, aes192-ctr and aes128-ctr.
rules.impact: Weak ciphers cannot provide confidentiality or integrity, so system data may be compromised. Triple DES ciphers allow a birthday attack on long encrypted sessions, and CBC mode error handling helps remote attackers recover cleartext data.

rules.title: Sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: ClientAliveInterval sets the timeout in seconds after which sshd requests a response from an idle client through the encrypted channel, and 0 disables the messages. ClientAliveCountMax sets how many client alive messages are sent without a response before sshd disconnects the client, and 0 disables termination.
rules.impact: Appropriate values for ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax prevent resource exhaustion. ClientAliveCountMax must be greater than zero for SSH to disconnect idle connections, and a 45-second timeout is one example.

rules.title: Sshd DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: The DisableForwarding parameter disables all forwarding features, including X11, ssh-agent, TCP and StreamLocal, and overrides all other forwarding-related options. It can simplify restricted configurations.
rules.impact: X11 forwarding carries a small risk that other users on the X11 server compromise the remote X11 servers of users who logged in with it. Port forwarding can expose the organization to backdoors and data exfiltration, because SSH encryption hides its contents from most network monitoring.

rules.title: Sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication via trusted hosts through a user .rhosts file or /etc/hosts.equiv is permitted, along with successful public key authentication of the client host.
rules.impact: Although .rhosts files are ineffective if support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use them in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.

rules.title: Sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files are not used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter forces users to enter a password when authenticating with SSH.

rules.title: Sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: Only ecdh-sha2-nistp256, ecdh-sha2-nistp384, ecdh-sha2-nistp521, diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256, diffie-hellman-group16-sha512, diffie-hellman-group18-sha512 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 are approved key exchange algorithms under FIPS 140-2. Earlier algorithms in the KexAlgorithms list are preferred.
rules.impact: Key exchange methods that are considered weak must be removed, because a method may use too few bits or a hashing algorithm that is too weak. Using weak algorithms can lead to man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: Sshd LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication of the SSH server. The longer the grace period, the longer unauthenticated connections can exist.
rules.impact: A low LoginGraceTime minimizes the risk of successful brute force attacks against the SSH server and limits the number of simultaneous unauthenticated connections. The recommended setting is 60 seconds, subject to site policy.

rules.title: Sshd LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: LogLevel gives the level of verbosity used when logging messages from sshd. The possible values are QUIET, FATAL, ERROR, INFO, VERBOSE and the DEBUG levels, the default is INFO, and logging at the DEBUG level violates the privacy of users and is not recommended.
rules.impact: The DEBUG levels are not recommended except for debugging SSH communications, because they hide critical security information in a mass of data and can fill the available disk space. The VERBOSE level logs login and logout activity plus the key fingerprint of SSH keys.

rules.title: Sshd MACs are configured
rules.explanation: This variable limits the types of MAC algorithms that SSH can use during communication, and some organizations have stricter requirements for approved MACs. The only strong MACs currently approved by FIPS 140-2 are HMAC-SHA1, HMAC-SHA2-256, HMAC-SHA2-384 and HMAC-SHA2-512.
rules.impact: MD5 and 96-bit MAC algorithms are considered weak and increase exploitability in SSH attacks. An attacker who breaks the algorithm can use a man-in-the-middle position to decrypt the SSH tunnel and capture credentials and information.

rules.title: Sshd MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter limits the number of authentication attempts allowed per connection, and failures beyond half that number are written to syslog.
rules.impact: A low MaxAuthTries value reduces the risk of a successful brute force attack against the SSH server; 4 is the recommended value, subject to site policy.

rules.title: Sshd MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxSessions parameter limits the number of open sessions allowed on a single connection.
rules.impact: Rate limiting with MaxSessions protects sshd login availability and keeps many simultaneous sessions from overwhelming the daemon.

rules.title: Sshd MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxStartups parameter limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections to the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: Rate limiting with MaxStartups protects sshd login availability and keeps pending authentication attempts from overwhelming the daemon.

rules.title: Sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter controls whether the SSH server accepts logins to accounts with empty password strings.
rules.impact: Refusing remote access to accounts with an empty password reduces the likelihood of unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: Sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitRootLogin parameter controls whether root can log in over SSH; the default is prohibit-password.
rules.impact: Refusing direct root login over SSH makes administrators authenticate with their own account before escalating, which supports verification during a security incident.

rules.title: Sshd PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment option allows users to present environment options to the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: User-supplied environment variables can bypass security controls, for example by setting an execution path that makes SSH run a trojan program.

rules.title: Sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the PAM interface, which adds PAM account and session processing for all authentication types.
rules.impact: With PAM enabled, account and session checks run properly, so access can be restricted by IP, time or other account factors and the login environment can be controlled.

rules.title: Sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo lets a permitted user run a command as the superuser or another user, as defined by the security policy.
rules.impact: The sudoers policy in /usr/local/etc/sudoers and /usr/local/etc/sudoers.d determines which privileges a user may exercise and can require password authentication.

rules.title: Sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: sudo can be configured to run only from a pseudo-terminal.
rules.impact: Without use_pty, a malicious program run through sudo can fork a background process that keeps running after the main program exits.

rules.title: Sudo log file exists
rules.explanation: The Defaults logfile entry sets the path of the sudo log file; setting the path enables file logging, and sudo otherwise logs through syslog.
rules.impact: A dedicated sudo log file simplifies auditing of sudo commands and the creation of verified rules for sudo.

rules.title: Users must provide a password for escalation
rules.explanation: The system must be configured so that users provide a password when they escalate privileges.
rules.impact: Without re-authentication, users can reach resources or perform tasks for which they are not authorized.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: The system must require users to re-confirm their authenticity when they escalate privileges.
rules.impact: Without re-authentication, users can access resources or perform tasks beyond their authorization.

rules.title: Sudo authentication timeout is configured correctly
rules.explanation: sudo caches credentials for 5 minutes by default; timestamp_timeout in /usr/local/etc/sudoers changes the timeout in line with local security policy.
rules.impact: A short timeout reduces the chance of unauthorized privileged access through a cached credential.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command lets a user run a command or shell as another user and is normally open to all users; enabling pam_wheel.so in /etc/pam.d/su limits su to a group, which should be empty to reinforce sudo use.
rules.impact: Restricting su and using sudo instead gives administrators better control over privilege escalation and a per-command audit trail, whereas su records only that the su program ran.

rules.title: Password length is configured
rules.explanation: minlen sets the minimum acceptable length for a new password, with separate N0 to N4 limits for one to four character classes, N2 for passphrases and the disabled keyword to reject a password type.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect the system from brute force attacks.

rules.title: Password quality is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: The pam_passwdqc enforce=everyone option makes the module return an error when a password check fails, even for root; it is disabled by default, so root otherwise sees only a message and can still set the password.
rules.impact: Password quality checks applied to root increase the time and resources needed to crack a password, since a more complex password has more possible combinations.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include nullok
rules.explanation: The nullok argument overrides the default of pam_unix.so, which denies service access to users whose official password is blank.
rules.impact: A blank password lets unauthorized users reach personal and confidential information.

rules.title: Strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: The passwd_format setting in /etc/login.conf selects the hash for local passwords; SHA-512 provides a stronger hash than the other algorithms FreeBSD uses.
rules.impact: A stronger hash raises the effort needed to determine local user passwords from a stolen hash; the setting applies only to the local system.

rules.title: Password expiration is 365 days or less
rules.explanation: The passwordtime parameter in /etc/login.conf forces passwords to expire after a set age and must be 365 days or less.
rules.impact: A shorter maximum password age limits the window in which an attacker can use compromised credentials or succeed at an online brute force attack.

rules.title: Password expiration warning days is 7 or more
rules.explanation: The warnpassword parameter in /etc/login.conf tells users that their password expires in a set number of days and is recommended to be 7 or more.
rules.impact: Advance warning gives users time to choose a secure password instead of picking a simple one or writing it down.

rules.title: Default group for the root account is GID 0
rules.explanation: The root account must belong to group GID 0, which affects the permissions of files that root creates.
rules.impact: GID 0 for the root account helps prevent accidental access to root-owned files by unprivileged users.

rules.title: Root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The umask sets permissions on newly created files and directories, which default to 0644 and 0755 in FreeBSD; the root umask is set in /root/.profile and /root/.shrc, with /root/.profile taking precedence.
rules.impact: A permissive umask can create directories and files with excessive permissions that unauthorized users can read or write.

rules.title: System accounts are secured
rules.explanation: System accounts manage applications and are not intended to provide an interactive shell; their password field in /etc/master.passwd is set to an invalid string and their shell field should be nologin.
rules.impact: Setting the shell field to nologin prevents a system account from being used to run commands.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: /etc/shells lists the full pathnames of valid login shells and is consulted by chsh and by other programs such as FTP daemons, which deny users whose shell is absent.
rules.impact: A shell that is not in /etc/shells marks a restricted account, so listing nologin there makes nologin users appear as full, unrestricted users.

rules.title: Default user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The umask sets permissions on newly created files and directories, which default to 0644 and 0755 in FreeBSD; the default comes from UMASK in /etc/login.conf or from /etc/profile and /etc/csh.cshrc, and scripts in /etc/profile.d/*.sh take precedence.
rules.impact: A permissive umask can create files and directories with excessive permissions readable or writable by unauthorized users.

rules.title: Syslog is installed
rules.explanation: syslogd ships with the FreeBSD base system and is the recommended logging daemon.
rules.impact: The syslogd utility reads and writes messages to the system console, log files, other machines and users as specified in its configuration file.

rules.title: Syslogd service is enabled
rules.explanation: The syslogd service is enabled at boot through the sysrc parameter syslogd_enable.
rules.impact: If syslogd is not enabled at boot, the system records no logging events.

rules.title: Syslogd default file permissions are configured
rules.explanation: syslogd creates log files that do not yet exist, and /etc/newsyslog.conf sets the permissions applied to them; newsyslog also handles rotation and retention.
rules.impact: Correct log file permissions support archiving and protect sensitive data.

rules.title: Logging is configured
rules.explanation: Logging rules and the files used for each class of message are defined in /etc/syslog.conf, /etc/syslog.d/*.conf and /usr/local/etc/syslog.d/*.conf.
rules.impact: syslog carries security-relevant events such as successful and failed su attempts, failed logins and attempts to log in as root.

rules.title: Syslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
rules.explanation: Syslog can send collected events to a remote log host and can receive messages from remote hosts, which allows centralized log management.
rules.impact: Log data stored on a remote host resists tampering by an attacker who gains root locally and can otherwise alter or delete local logs.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive logs from a remote client
rules.explanation: Syslog can act as a log server by receiving messages from remote hosts; the syslogd_flags parameter -s prevents a client from receiving data from other hosts.
rules.impact: A client configured to receive data becomes a server and operates outside its intended operating boundary.

rules.title: Newsyslog is configured
rules.explanation: Log rotation keeps logs from filling the system or growing unmanageably large and is configured in /etc/newsyslog.conf, /etc/newsyslog.conf.d/*.conf and /usr/local/etc/newsyslog.conf.d/*.conf.
rules.impact: Smaller, rotated logs are easier to archive to another system and take less time to review.

rules.title: All logfiles have appropriate access configured
rules.explanation: Log files in /var/log hold information from many system services and possibly from other logged hosts.
rules.impact: Log files need the correct permissions to protect sensitive data and allow access only to the appropriate users and groups.

rules.title: Auditd service is enabled
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon records system events and is enabled through the sysrc parameter auditd_enable.
rules.impact: Captured system events give administrators the information needed to determine whether unauthorized access has occurred.

rules.title: Audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: The filesz parameter in /etc/security/audit_control sets the maximum audit log file size; a full log is rotated and a new log file is started.
rules.impact: An appropriate size keeps log files from affecting the system and prevents loss of audit data.

rules.title: Audit logs are not automatically deleted
rules.explanation: The expire-after parameter in /etc/security/audit_control sets when audit log files expire and are deleted; audit logs are not deleted automatically.
rules.impact: In high-security conditions the benefit of a long audit history outweighs the cost of storing that history.

rules.title: Actions as another user are always logged
rules.explanation: Sudo grants temporary elevated privileges to run operations as the superuser or another user; the aa event class records these actions in the audit trail.
rules.impact: An audit trail of elevated operations supports accountability, and administrators correlate audit events with the sudo log to verify whether unauthorized commands ran.
rules.scope: aa event class in flags audit_control

rules.title: Events that modify the sudo log file are collected
rules.explanation: When su is restricted and administrators use sudo, privileged commands are logged to /var/log/sudo.log; each command opens the file for writing and triggers an audit event.
rules.impact: Changes to /var/log/sudo.log show that an administrator ran a command or that the log was tampered with, and can be correlated with the audit trail.
rules.scope: fa,fc,fd,fm,fr,fw event classes in flags audit_control

rules.title: Use of privileged commands is collected
rules.explanation: This rule monitors privileged programs, those with the setuid or setgid bit set, to determine whether unprivileged users execute them.
rules.impact: Execution of a privileged command by an unprivileged user may indicate an attempt to gain unauthorized access to the system.
rules.scope: pc event class in flags audit_control

rules.title: Discretionary access control permission modification events are collected
rules.explanation: This rule tracks system calls that change file permissions, attributes, ownership and group, including chmod, chown, setxattr and removexattr, and writes a record only for non-system user IDs.
rules.impact: Monitoring attribute changes can alert the administrator to activity that indicates attacker activity or a policy violation.

rules.title: Successful file system mounts are collected
rules.explanation: This rule monitors the mount and umount system calls and generates an audit record when an unprivileged user mounts a file system.
rules.impact: Unprivileged mounts are unusual and give the administrator evidence that removable media was mounted, though not that data was written to it.
rules.scope: ad event class in flags audit_control

rules.title: Login and logout events are collected
rules.explanation: This rule monitors login and logout events through the lo event class.
rules.impact: Login and logout records give the administrator information about brute-force attacks on user logins.
rules.scope: lo event class in flags audit_control

rules.title: File deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: This rule monitors the unlink, unlinkat, rename and renameat system calls, which delete or rename files and file attributes, and tags them with the identifier delete.
rules.impact: Monitoring these calls by unprivileged users shows improper deletion of protected files, and administrators then look for specific privileged files being deleted or modified.
rules.scope: fd event class in flags audit_control

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are recorded
rules.explanation: The system must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful use of the usermod command through the aa and ad event classes.
rules.impact: Without audit records that meet security needs, correlating and investigating incident events, or identifying those responsible, is difficult.
rules.scope: aa/ad classes in flags audit_control (user changes)

rules.title: The audit log directory is 0750 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The audit log directory contains the audit log files and must be mode 0750 or more restrictive.
rules.impact: Audit records, settings and reports must be protected from unauthorized modification or deletion, since compromise prevents forensic analysis of malicious activity.

rules.title: Audit log files are mode 0640 or less permissive
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity and must be mode 0640 or less permissive.
rules.impact: Access to audit records exposes system and configuration data to attackers, which can compromise its confidentiality.

rules.title: Only authorized users own audit log files
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity and must be owned only by authorized users.
rules.impact: Access to audit records exposes system and configuration data to attackers, which can compromise its confidentiality.

rules.title: Only authorized groups are assigned ownership of audit log files
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity and must belong only to authorized groups.
rules.impact: Access to audit records exposes system and configuration data to attackers, which can compromise its confidentiality.
rules.scope: Owner group of audit log files

rules.title: Audit configuration files are restrictive
rules.explanation: The audit configuration files in /etc/security/audit* control what is audited and which events are checked.
rules.impact: Access to these files can let unauthorized personnel prevent auditing of critical events; a bad configuration can also overload the audit log or hinder incident investigation.

rules.title: Audit configuration files are owned by root
rules.explanation: The audit configuration files in /etc/security/audit* control what is audited and which events are checked.
rules.impact: Access to these files can let unauthorized personnel prevent auditing of critical events; a bad configuration can also overload the audit log or hinder incident investigation.

rules.title: Audit configuration files belong to group wheel
rules.explanation: The audit configuration files in /etc/security/audit* control what is audited and which events are checked.
rules.impact: Access to these files can let unauthorized personnel prevent auditing of critical events; a bad configuration can also overload the audit log or hinder incident investigation.

rules.title: Audit tools are 555 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: Audit tools include vendor-supplied and open source utilities needed to view and manipulate audit activity and records, plus custom queries and report generators.
rules.impact: Protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data prevents unauthorized operation on audit information.

rules.title: Audit tools are owned by root
rules.explanation: Audit tools in /usr/sbin include the utilities needed to view and manipulate audit activity and records, including custom queries and report generators.
rules.impact: Protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data prevents unauthorized operation on audit information.

rules.title: Audit tools belong to group wheel
rules.explanation: Audit tools in /usr/sbin include the utilities needed to view and manipulate audit activity and records, including custom queries and report generators.
rules.impact: Protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data prevents unauthorized operation on audit information.

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: AIDE is an intrusion detection tool that uses predefined rules and its own database to check the integrity of files and directories.
rules.impact: Comparing the stored snapshot of modification times, permissions and hashes against the current file system detects compromised files and limits the impact of tampering.

rules.title: Filesystem integrity is regularly checked
rules.explanation: Periodic file system integrity checks are necessary to detect changes in the file system.
rules.impact: Regular checks let the administrator determine whether critical files were changed in an unauthorized manner.
rules.scope: root crontab with an aide job

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file holds user account information used by many system utilities and must stay readable for those utilities to work.
rules.impact: /etc/passwd must be protected from unauthorized write access; permissions are correct by default but can change unintentionally or through malicious action.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/group are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file lists all valid groups and allows read and write access for root and read access for everyone else.
rules.impact: The /etc/group file must be protected from unauthorized changes by unprivileged users and must stay readable, since many unprivileged programs use it.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/master.passwd are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/master.passwd file stores account information critical to account security, including the hashed password and expiration data.
rules.impact: Access to /etc/master.passwd lets an attacker run a password cracking program against the hash and use other stored data to compromise accounts.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shells are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shells lists the full pathnames of valid login shells and is consulted by chsh and by other programs.
rules.impact: /etc/shells must be protected from unauthorized access; permissions are correct by default but can change unintentionally or through malicious action.

rules.title: World writable files and directories are secured
rules.explanation: World-writable files can be modified by any user on the system, and the sticky bit on a world-writable directory prevents users from deleting or renaming files they do not own.
rules.impact: Writable data can be modified or compromised by any local user and may point to a poorly written script, which can lead to greater compromise of system integrity.

rules.title: No unowned or ungrouped files or directories exist
rules.explanation: Administrators may remove users or groups without removing the files and directories those users or groups own.
rules.impact: A new user or group assigned the reused ID can own the removed user's files and gain more access to the system than intended.
rules.scope: Files/directories without an owner or group (find -nouser/-nogroup)

rules.title: SUID and SGID files are reviewed
rules.explanation: A file owner can set permissions so the file runs with the owner's or group's privileges; SUID and SGID are commonly used for functions such as changing a password that require root.
rules.impact: Reviewing SUID and SGID files confirms they are legitimate, and a binary whose checksum differs from the package may have been replaced.
rules.scope: Files with the SUID/SGID bits set

rules.title: Accounts in /etc/master.passwd use shadowed passwords
rules.explanation: Shadowed passwords are stored in /etc/master.passwd as a salted one-way hash; /etc/passwd carries an asterisk in its password field instead of the hash.
rules.impact: Shadowing moves password hashes to a file only root can read, which reduces the risk of a dictionary attack against a world-readable /etc/passwd.

rules.title: Password fields in /etc/master.passwd are not empty
rules.explanation: An account with an empty password field in /etc/master.passwd lets anyone log in as that user without providing a password.
rules.impact: Every account must have a password or be locked, so it cannot be used by an unauthorized user.

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: Administration errors and changes over time can leave groups defined in /etc/passwd but missing from /etc/group.
rules.impact: A group that exists only in /etc/passwd is a threat to system security, because its group permissions are not managed properly.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: The adduser and pw programs reject duplicate UIDs, but an administrator can edit /etc/passwd and change the UID field manually.
rules.impact: Unique UIDs are required for accountability and appropriate access protection.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: The pw program rejects a duplicate GID, but an administrator can edit /etc/group and change the GID field manually.
rules.impact: Unique GIDs are required for accountability and proper access protection.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: The adduser and pw programs reject duplicate user names, but an administrator can edit /etc/passwd and change the name manually.
rules.impact: With a duplicate name, the user creates and accesses files with the first UID for that name, so the UID is effectively shared, which is a security problem.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: The groupadd program rejects duplicate group names, but an administrator can edit /etc/group and change the name manually.
rules.impact: With a duplicate name, the group creates and accesses files with the first GID for that name, so the GID is effectively shared.

rules.title: Integrity of the root PATH
rules.explanation: The root user can execute any command and can be tricked into running a program unintentionally if PATH is not set correctly.
rules.impact: A current working directory or another writable directory in the root PATH lets an attacker gain superuser access by making an administrator run a trojan horse.
rules.scope: PATH variable of the root user

rules.title: Root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: Any account with UID 0 has superuser privileges on the system.
rules.impact: Access should be limited to the root account from the system console, with administrative work done from an unprivileged account and access to su restricted.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories are configured
rules.explanation: A home directory holds a user's local environment settings and personal files; users can be defined in /etc/passwd without a home directory or with one that does not exist.
rules.impact: The user must own the directory, since group or world writable home directories let attackers steal or modify other users' data or gain their privileges.

rules.title: Local interactive user dot files access is configured
rules.explanation: Users can override permissions that the administrator sets on dot files; .forward forwards mail, .rhost defines trusted hosts for rlogin, rsh and rcp, .netrc holds login data and the shell history file records recent commands.
rules.impact: Excessively permissive dot files let attackers steal or modify other users' data or gain another user's system privileges.
